one_liner: Lua 5.3 dialect with optional static types and a MIR-based JIT; typed numeric loops ran 10-26x faster than Lua 5.3.2 (old LLVM backend).
what_it_does: Ravi is a fork of the Lua 5.3 VM, embedded through the usual Lua C API, that adds optional type annotations (integer, number, integer[], number[], table, string, closures, userdata), typed array constructors and slices, a defer statement and Lua 5.4's generational GC. Untyped Lua 5.3 programs run unchanged in interpreted mode; typed code makes the parser emit type-specialised bytecodes. A JIT compiles functions on request (ravi.compile, the default manual mode) or automatically (ravi.auto), and a separate alpha compiler framework can AOT-compile Ravi source to shared libraries and accept embedded C snippets.
how_it_is_fast: Type annotations let the front end emit specialised bytecodes (integer/float arithmetic, typed array get/set, integer for-loops) that skip Lua's dynamic tag checks, with runtime type assertions where values cross from untyped code. The bytecode JIT translates each compiled function's bytecode to C source and compiles it in-process with MIR's c2mir and MIR generator (optimisation level 0-3, default 2); the published numbers came from the earlier LLVM 3.9 backend. An omitArrayGetRangeCheck compile option drops bounds checks on typed array reads.
when_to_use: Numeric loops in embedded Lua 5.3 code where you can annotate locals and arrays as integer, number, integer[] or number[] and pre-compile the hot functions at startup.
You need Lua 5.3 semantics (64-bit integers, integer division, utf8, 5.3 C API) that LuaJIT's Lua 5.1 dialect does not provide, with JIT speed on typed hot paths.
Hosts on Linux or macOS that can ship a shared library with a vendored JIT (MIR is bundled; no LLVM dependency any more).
Projects that want to AOT-compile some Ravi modules to native shared libraries or inline small C snippets (alpha compiler framework).
when_not_to_use: Untyped Lua code: in the author's table the JIT gains only 1.6-2.5x over Lua 5.3.2 on untyped mandel, fannkuchen and matmul, and LuaJIT 2.1 is about 5-16x faster than the Ravi JIT on those same untyped programs (derived from page data).
Windows with JIT: the MIR build instructions say the JIT does not work correctly on Windows (stack unwinding), although the published benchmarks were run on Windows with the old LLVM backend.

Coroutine-heavy, tail-recursive or debug-hook code: JIT code runs only on the main thread (coroutines are interpreted), JIT tail calls are plain calls limited to about 110 deep, and the debug API and hooks are unavailable in JIT mode.
Code that needs a fast C FFI or cross-function inlining; the benchmark page notes Ravi has neither, unlike LuaJIT.
Programs near Lua's parser limits: Ravi halves MAXUPVAL, MAXREGS, MAXVARS and LUAI_MAXCCALLS to about 125, and its bytecode is incompatible with Lua 5.x.

integration.dependencies: none external for the default build (MIR/c2mir vendored); readline for the REPL on some Linux builds (issue #254)
integration.min_toolchain: C99, CMake 3.12+; Visual Studio 2019 documented for Windows (interpreter only in practice)
integration.platforms: Interpreter: portable C99 (Linux, macOS, Windows). MIR JIT: Linux and macOS; not reliable on Windows per ravi-mir-instructions.rst. CPU architectures for the JIT follow MIR's backends (not documented in the Ravi pages read).
integration.thread_safety: Same model as Lua 5.3: one lua_State per thread, no shared-state locking; JIT state is per global_State (not documented beyond this)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — runs Lua 5.3 source in interpreted mode and keeps the Lua 5.3 C API, but bytecode is incompatible, several limits are halved, the GC interface follows Lua 5.4, and the speedups need type annotations plus explicit ravi.compile calls

gotchas: Harness flaws behind the headline ratios: fornum_test1 (29x) is a dead-store loop (j = i for 1e9 iterations, returning only the last value), so it times empty-loop overhead (0.309 s, about 0.3 ns per iteration); fornum_test3 likewise overwrites j in an inner 3-iteration loop. They show JIT loop overhead, not useful work.

The 26x typed matmul figure (matmul1.ravi, 1.039 s) is a different program from matmul1.lua: it stores matrices as flat 1-D number arrays (matrix.mul2/gen2) instead of tables of rows and compiles with omitArrayGetRangeCheck=1; matmul1_ravi.lua (1.137 s) is the closer typed port. The current fannkuchen.ravi and mandel1.ravi also pass omitArrayGetRangeCheck=1, which the page mentions only for matmul.

All published numbers are from about 2016 on the archived LLVM 3.9 backend with JIT compile time excluded (ravi.compile runs before the os.clock window, and LuaJIT gets one untimed warm-up run); no numbers exist for the current MIR backend, whose code path (bytecode to C to c2mir) is different.

A 2026-09-12 interpreter review in the repo (readthedocs/INTERPRETER_REVIEW.md) found typed integer-array stores silently truncating floats, 64-bit array indices narrowed to 32 bits before the bounds check (a[4294967297] aliased a[1]), fixed-size arrays growing, and a coroutine/defer use-after-realloc crash; commits the same day say they fixed all four (#267-#270), so older builds carry them.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Ravi over LuaJIT Remake (Deegen) when you need Lua 5.3 semantics, an embeddable C library with optional typing and a JIT/AOT path rather than a faster Lua 5.1 interpreter; pick Terra instead when you want explicitly staged low-level code generated from Lua rather than a typed Lua dialect.
verified_claims_summary: The author's 2016-era table (readthedocs/ravi-benchmarks.rst, llvm branch) times numeric scripts on Windows 10 64-bit, unknown CPU, Visual C++ 2015 builds of Lua 5.3.2 and Ravi, LLVM 3.9 JIT, compile time excluded: typed mandel1 1.571 s, fannkuchen 4.634 s and matmul 1.039 s versus untyped Lua 5.3.2 runs of 20.324, 46.203 and 26.672 s (about 13x, 10x, 26x, derived from page data), roughly matching LuaJIT 2.1 (1.594, 4.672, 1.078 s). Untyped code under the Ravi JIT gains only 1.6-2.5x, and the Ravi interpreter alone is within about 5% of Lua 5.3.2.
status_note: Sporadically maintained (bursts in June 2024, February 2025 and September 2026, 95 open issues) and MIT-licensed; usable as a Lua 5.3 replacement library, but its performance claims describe a backend that was archived in 2020 and nobody has published MIR-era numbers.
